title: Relay WhatsApp business messaging system

context.problem: Relay must give a Frappe user a realtime, permission-safe WhatsApp inbox centred on a business document that can have multiple contacts, while Relay Hub durably accepts provider and outbound traffic for up to 100 sites. The present split between Hub transport and Core business context is sound, but duplicate channel activation, scan-based callback dispatch, and a shared slow Core queue make setup ambiguous and the live path fail its stated latency and throughput goals.
constraints: Frappe v16 Core and Go Hub remain separate deployable applications
WhatsApp-only product scope for the current milestone
Hub uses PostgreSQL durable queues; Core uses MariaDB, Frappe RQ and Frappe Socket.IO
100 sites, up to 50 provider submissions/s per site, and a 1,000,000-intent aggregate burst are user-stated targets
status callbacks are compact batches of at most 500 records and 512 KiB
incremental migration; no rewrite and no new broker without measurement

functional.text: Open a WhatsApp conversation by business document and choose among its linked contacts and mobile endpoints.
Accept inbound messages immediately, persist them before provider acknowledgement, project them to Core and update open inboxes through Socket.IO.
Send text and WhatsApp media/template messages with optimistic Sending, then Sent, Delivered, Read or Failed states.
Load history with cursor-based reverse infinite scrolling, restore each user's position and track per-user read state.
Enforce Frappe business-document, Contact, group-claim and assignment permissions on every list, read and send API.
Manage Meta WhatsApp credentials, webhook verification, phone identity and templates through one activation lifecycle.
Support canned replies, AI summaries and configurable flows after the base message path is healthy.

priorities.rationale: The user repeatedly prioritised realtime correctness, optimized throughput and a system that remains responsive during large bursts.

conflicts.text: Core Relay Channel and Hub channel credentials both currently express account activation.
conflicts.resolution: Hub becomes the transport activation authority; Core keeps a derived capability projection and site binding only.

conflicts.text: The user asks for 5,000 provider submissions/s, while the checked Hub benchmark sustained 32.5/s and Meta quotas are not configured.
conflicts.resolution: Treat 5,000/s as a capacity target behind admission control, and require provider-quota and worker measurements before claiming it.

conflicts.text: Current Core documentation describes realtime delivery, but inbound projection is queued on the shared long queue and may be delayed by AI or reports.
conflicts.resolution: Move realtime projection to a dedicated high-priority queue and measure callback-to-browser latency.

interfaces.deadline: persist and respond within 250 ms target
interfaces.retryability: Meta retries; Hub never retries the HTTP response
interfaces.backpressure: bounded request body and four current ingress workers; return 429/5xx before commit when saturated

interfaces.name: Hub realtime callback
interfaces.transport: authenticated HTTPS batch from Hub to Core
interfaces.consistency: at-least-once until Core durably records every event
interfaces.idempotency: Hub event id unique in Core
interfaces.trustBoundary: Hub callback worker → Frappe whitelisted endpoint with callback secret
interfaces.deadline: 1 s maximum event age target; 3 s HTTP timeout
interfaces.retryability: Hub owns retry with exponential jitter and durable cursor
interfaces.backpressure: at most 50 events/call; per-site circuit breaker and bounded unacknowledged retention
interfaces.compatibility: version field; reader-first rollout and unknown additive fields ignored
interfaces.failureResult: Core returns highest contiguous acknowledged cursor; timeout leaves events pending

interfaces.name: Hub status callback
interfaces.transport: authenticated HTTPS compact batch from Hub to Core
interfaces.purpose: advance sent, delivered, read and failed receipts
interfaces.trustBoundary: Hub callback worker → Core callback API
interfaces.deadline: 5 s maximum status age target; 5 s HTTP timeout
interfaces.retryability: Hub owns retry from status cursor
interfaces.backpressure: 500 statuses and 512 KiB per call; backlog retained and chunked
interfaces.compatibility: versioned compact schema; Core accepts old and new fields during rolling deploy
interfaces.failureResult: partial batches are rejected atomically and retried; monotonic older states are harmless

interfaces.name: Browser realtime invalidation
interfaces.transport: Frappe Socket.IO event plus authenticated delta fetch
interfaces.consistency: payload-free invalidation followed by permission-checked read-your-projection fetch
interfaces.trustBoundary: Core realtime server → authenticated Frappe browser session
interfaces.retryability: browser reconnect performs cursor resync; server does not replay socket frames
interfaces.backpressure: coalesce invalidations per conversation; delta page maximum 50 and DOM window 150
interfaces.compatibility: event names versioned; delta endpoint tolerates additive fields
interfaces.failureResult: missed socket event is repaired by reconnect resync without polling

deepDives.title: One authority for WhatsApp activation
deepDives.pressure: A channel can be configured in Hub while Core Relay Channel remains disabled or points elsewhere, producing ambiguous 403/404 and uncategorized events.
deepDives.decision: Hub owns credentials and the DRAFT-to-ACTIVE state machine. Core stores only its account binding and a derived capability projection returned by Hub.
alternatives: Keep manual configuration in both applications
Move provider secrets into every Core site
deepDives.failureMode: Hub accepts a webhook for an account that Core cannot route, or Core offers send for a channel Hub has not activated.
evidence: current Relay Settings plus Relay Channel schema

deepDives.title: Event-driven callback scheduling and isolated projection
deepDives.pressure: The current eight-worker 250 ms account scan has a 3.25 s lower bound across 100 accounts, and Core projection shares the long queue with AI and reports.
deepDives.decision: Upsert a due account/lane row when the webhook transaction commits; claim due rows fairly with SKIP LOCKED, and hand Core events to a dedicated high-priority projector queue.
alternatives: Increase polling frequency and worker count
Add Kafka between Hub and Core
deepDives.failureMode: An admitted inbound message remains durable but invisible while empty accounts are scanned or slow AI work occupies every Core long worker.
evidence: Core projection enqueued on Frappe long queue

deepDives.title: Bound the million-intent burst
deepDives.pressure: One million 2–4 KiB intents create 2–4 GB raw writes and take 8.55 hours at the measured 32.5/s versus 3.33 minutes at the stated target.
deepDives.decision: Preserve the PostgreSQL outbox, enforce per-account and global admission bounds, schedule fairly by account, and scale Hub workers horizontally only after Meta quota and provider-latency measurements justify it.
alternatives: Buffer the burst in process memory
deepDives.failureMode: Retries amplify offered load while the provider slows, exhausting connections, WAL or disk and starving small accounts behind one hot tenant.

pros: One activation state prevents Hub/Core configuration drift
Due-work claims remove the 100-account scan floor while preserving PostgreSQL recovery
Dedicated Core projection capacity protects chat latency from slow AI and reporting jobs
Bulkheads and explicit admission bounds make provider slowdown survivable without a new broker
cons: Adds lifecycle and scheduling state that operators must observe
The 5,000/s drain goal still depends on Meta quota and measured horizontal worker capacity
PostgreSQL remains a regional failure domain until standby and restore drills are operated

notes: Add activation_version/state and due schedule rows additively in Hub; old scan workers continue reading existing cursors.
Deploy Core callback readers and dedicated projector workers before Hub writes the versioned callback envelope.
Backfill due rows from unacknowledged cursors, compare shadow lag, then disable fixed account scans.
Project Hub capability state into Core, stop manual Relay Channel writes, and retain rollback until every site reports ACTIVE through Hub.

reasoning: nfr-2 requires p99 inbound visibility under 1 second, but the current 100-account scan alone has a 3.25 second lower bound; due-work scheduling removes that empty-account scan.
fr-6 requires usable Meta setup, and one Hub-owned activation state gives the invariant one enforcement authority instead of two editable records.

nfr-4 requires bounded behavior during a million-intent burst; the existing durable PostgreSQL outbox plus explicit per-account/global admission is sufficient, while a new broker has no measured bottleneck to solve.
Separating Core projection from AI/report work contains the named queue-starvation failure without changing the Hub/Core domain boundary.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Core and Hub can disagree about whether the WhatsApp channel is active

evidence.text: Core stores account binding in Relay Settings and editable channel enablement in Relay Channel, while Hub separately stores account and provider credentials.
evidence.source: relay_core DocType schemas; relay_hub internal/store/schema.go and account UI

findings.whyItMatters: It violates fr-6 and allows webhook acceptance, inbox availability and send availability to disagree for the same account.

remedy.text: Make Hub the only activation authority and project a read-only capability state into Core.

findings.blastRadius: WhatsApp setup, webhook routing and send eligibility
findings.disconfirming: The records serve different domains, but both currently contain operator-editable enablement rather than an explicit source/derived contract.

lenses.objection: A derived Core cache would be valid, but the current schema and setup flow do not enforce derivation.
No accepted ADR documents intentional dual control or conflict resolution.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Realtime message projection shares the slow queue with AI and reporting work

evidence.text: Incoming Hub events enqueue relay_core.automation.projection.project on Frappe's long queue, which also carries AI summaries, campaigns, translations and flows.
evidence.source: relay_core callbacks/projection modules and queue configuration

findings.whyItMatters: A slow unrelated job can violate nfr-2 even when Hub delivers the event on time.

remedy.text: Create a dedicated high-priority projection queue and workers, with lag alerts and a durable Relay Hub Event recovery scan.

findings.blastRadius: inbound messages, receipts and live inbox updates
findings.disconfirming: Low current traffic may hide starvation, but sharing all workers leaves no enforceable latency bound.

lenses.objection: RQ priorities could help only if dedicated capacity and starvation behavior were configured; they are not.
No documented trade-off accepts AI work delaying inbound chat.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Account scanning cannot meet the realtime target at the stated tenant count

evidence.text: Realtime callbacks run on 250 ms ticks with eight workers; scanning 100 accounts takes at least 3.25 seconds before network and Core projection.

findings.whyItMatters: The scheduler alone exceeds nfr-2 by more than three times.

remedy.text: Replace full-account ticks with a transactional due account/lane index claimed fairly using SKIP LOCKED.

findings.disconfirming: More workers shorten the scan temporarily, but cost grows with inactive accounts and still lacks a due-work invariant.

lenses.objection: The computation is a lower bound and does not rely on a production latency sample.
No requirement accepts multi-second idle-account scan delay.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Measured provider drain is two orders below the stated aggregate target

evidence.text: The checked 2,000-message burst sustained 32.5/s, while nfr-5 asks for 5,000/s and the process caps the adaptive pool at eight workers.

findings.whyItMatters: At the measured rate a one-million-intent burst drains in 8.55 hours, violating nfr-5 and making retry amplification dangerous.

remedy.text: Partition fair worker capacity by account, add horizontal Hub process scaling and admit only measured Meta quota; retain the PostgreSQL outbox.

findings.blastRadius: outbound message latency and database backlog
findings.disconfirming: The local benchmark may understate production capacity and Meta may impose lower limits, but neither possibility supports the current 5,000/s claim.

lenses.objection: A provider quota below 5,000/s would require revising the target, not declaring the implementation compliant.
No production measurement demonstrates a different drain rate.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Cross-repository callback changes have no explicit version and rollout contract

evidence.text: Hub and Core deploy independently and callbacks use strict schemas, but the reviewed callback envelope and docs do not define a compatibility version or reader-first rollout window.
evidence.source: relay_hub callback worker and relay_core callback endpoints

findings.whyItMatters: An independently deployed writer can make Core reject all live events, violating nfr-2 until both repositories align.

remedy.text: Version the callback envelope, require additive reader-first changes, and run cross-version contract tests before deployment.

findings.disconfirming: Both applications may usually deploy together, but they are distinct repositories and no tool enforces lockstep release.

lenses.objection: Strict validation improves safety but turns harmless new fields into availability loss without a version rule.
No release contract was found in the owning documentation.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Durable event and message tables have no enforced retention steady state

evidence.text: Webhook events, outbox rows and Core business messages are durable, but reviewed schema and operations docs do not establish compaction or retention jobs.
evidence.source: Hub PostgreSQL schema; Core Relay DocTypes; operations docs

findings.whyItMatters: The million-intent burst adds gigabytes before WAL/index amplification, so repeated bursts eventually turn disk growth into an availability risk.

remedy.text: Define and implement retention by state: raw acknowledged events, resolved outbox, uncertain work and business messages each need separate policy and deletion proof.

findings.blastRadius: audit history, disk usage and deletion compliance
findings.disconfirming: The product may intentionally retain business history forever, but raw Hub transport journals still need an explicit lifecycle.

lenses.objection: Absence of a job is only debt because the declared burst makes unbounded growth material.

findings.subject: repo
findings.title: Database-disaster recovery targets are claimed without restore evidence

evidence.text: Hub production-gap documentation leaves backup/restore outstanding, and no Core restore drill tied to callback cursors was found.

findings.whyItMatters: It leaves nfr-7 unproven for the two stores that define acknowledged delivery and business history.

remedy.text: Automate backups and run a timed restore drill that replays Hub callbacks from durable cursors without duplicate business messages.

findings.blastRadius: all acknowledged provider events and business history after database loss
findings.disconfirming: Process crashes are covered by durable tables, but storage loss is the distinct failure named by the target.

lenses.objection: A configured backup is insufficient without a restore result and replay proof.
No accepted risk statement narrows nfr-7 to process loss only.

risks.text: Meta per-number and business limits may make the 5,000/s aggregate target impossible even after Hub scales; activation must measure and expose admitted quota.
A hot site can still dominate PostgreSQL WAL and disk; global and per-account watermarks must reject before the database loses recovery headroom.
Payload-free Socket.IO invalidation is safe only if reconnect delta APIs preserve a stable cursor and remain permission checked.
Retention values in this design are assumptions until product, audit and deletion requirements are agreed.

nextSteps: Implement and contract-test the Hub-owned WhatsApp activation state machine; make Core Relay Channel a derived read-only capability.
Add transactional due callback scheduling and benchmark 100 active plus 900 idle accounts against the p99 one-second inbound target.
Create a dedicated Core realtime projection queue/worker and measure callback commit-to-Socket.IO-visible latency under simultaneous AI/report load.
Version Hub callback envelopes and add reader-first cross-version tests spanning both repositories.
Run provider-backed outbound load tests to discover Meta quota and worker saturation; revise or prove the 5,000/s target before scaling infrastructure.
Define retention and execute PostgreSQL and MariaDB restore drills with callback replay and duplicate checks.
